readerTitle: Why Zara chose to guess less, not guess better
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Zara/Inditex) + 실제 연구 (Fisher 1997, Ferdows 외 2004) + 가상 적용 (베이커리 체인)
insight: 공급망이 빠르면 예측을 잘할 필요가 줄어든다. 리드타임을 줄이는 것은 미래를 덜 추측하는 방법이다.
misconception: 공급망의 목표는 언제나 단위 원가를 최저로 낮추는 것이고, 재고 문제는 예측을 더 정확하게 해서 푼다.

sources.text: Ferdows, K., Lewis, M. A., & Machuca, J. A. D. (2004). Rapid-Fire Fulfillment. Harvard Business Review. (주 2회 매장 배송, 소량 생산, 시즌 전 생산 확정 비중이 낮다는 점)
Ghemawat, P., & Nueno, J. L. (2003). ZARA: Fast Fashion. Harvard Business School case. (근거리 생산, 중앙 물류, 매장 피드백 구조)
Inditex annual reports (근거리 생산 'proximity sourcing' 비중과 생산 국가: 스페인, 포르투갈, 모로코, 튀르키예)
Fisher, M. L. (1997). What Is the Right Supply Chain for Your Product? Harvard Business Review. (효율형 vs 대응형 공급망)

factChecks.note: "새 아이템이 몇 주 안에 매장에 도착"은 자료마다 2~5주 등으로 다릅니다. 숫자 대신 "a few weeks"로만 썼습니다. 게시 전 Ferdows 외(2004)와 HBS 케이스로 재확인하세요.
근거리 생산 비중은 Inditex 연차보고서 기준으로 해마다 달라집니다(대략 절반 안팎으로 알려짐). 카드에는 "a large share"로만 적었습니다. 최신 보고서로 확인하세요.
주 2회 매장 배송은 Ferdows 외(2004)와 HBS 케이스에 나옵니다. 현재 운영과 다를 수 있으므로 "about twice a week" 및 과거형으로 적었습니다.
기본 상품(베이직)은 아시아 등 원거리·저가 공급처에서 생산한다는 점은 Ferdows 외(2004)에 서술되어 있습니다. 확인하세요.
Zara의 광고비가 업계 대비 낮다는 점은 널리 보도되었지만 이번 레슨에서는 다루지 않았습니다. 패스트패션의 환경 비판은 일반적 서술로만 썼습니다.
베이커리 체인 사례는 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why Zara chose to guess less, not guess better
body: For decades, most clothing brands planned their collections many months ahead. They placed big orders, shipped them across oceans, and hoped they had guessed right.
Zara, the Spanish fashion chain, built its business around a different idea. Its stores got new deliveries about twice a week.

image.label: A clothing store being restocked from a small delivery van
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 의류 매장 앞에 소형 배송 밴이 서 있고, 직원이 옷 몇 벌만 들고 들어가는 장면. 달력에 일주일에 두 번 체크 표시. 실제 브랜드 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where should your clothes be made?
body: You run a growing fashion chain. Far-away factories make clothes cheaply, but orders take months to arrive. Factories near your headquarters cost more per item, but can deliver in weeks.
Trends change fast, and you often end up discounting what didn't sell. What do you do?

options.text: Make everything far away. The lower cost per item is worth it
options.feedback: You win on cost per item, but you must commit months ahead. When you guess wrong, discounts and leftover stock can eat the savings.

options.text: Make trendy items nearby and steady basics far away
options.feedback: You pay more only where speed matters most. Basics sell predictably, so a long wait costs little there.

options.text: Make everything nearby so you can react to anything
options.feedback: You gain speed everywhere, but you pay the higher cost even on plain T-shirts that sell the same every season.

cards.title: It paid for speed where speed mattered.
body: Zara kept **a large share of its production close to home**, in Spain and nearby countries such as Portugal, Morocco and Turkey. Basics with steady demand came more often from cheaper, distant suppliers.
Goods flowed through central warehouses in Spain to stores worldwide. New designs launched in small first runs. A new piece could reach stores in a few weeks, not months.

cards.title: Lead time decides how much you have to guess
body: **Lead time** is the time between deciding to make something and having it ready to sell. The longer it is, the further ahead you must forecast, and the more often you guess wrong.
In a 1997 essay, researcher Marshall Fisher argued that products with unpredictable demand need a **responsive supply chain**: one built for speed and flexibility rather than lowest cost.

image.label: Two timelines: a long one full of guesses, a short one with few
image.brief: 두 개의 가로 타임라인 비교. 위쪽 긴 타임라인("Order 6 months ahead")에는 물음표가 많고, 아래 짧은 타임라인("Order a few weeks ahead")에는 물음표가 하나뿐. 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Sell first, then make more of what sells.
body: A short lead time changed how Zara could decide:
list: **Store managers** reported what customers bought and asked for
**Designers** adjusted styles based on those reports
**Small first runs** limited the cost of a miss
**More stock** went to what sold; what didn't was dropped
cards.callout: Instead of predicting a season, Zara could watch it and respond.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams use the same logic when they ship small changes often and watch usage. Short release cycles mean fewer big bets on what users might want.

cards.title: Match the supply chain to the product.
body: Zara did not make everything fast. Fisher's point was that one company can need two kinds of supply chain.

For steady products, such as basic T-shirts, cheap and slow works well, because forecasts are reliable. For products where demand is hard to predict, such as this season's trend, speed is worth paying for.
The mistake is running both kinds of product through the same chain.

cards.title: Speed has a price.
body: Making clothes nearby costs more per item, and frequent deliveries mean more transport. The model only pays off if fewer discounts and less unsold stock outweigh those costs.

It also demands tight coordination between stores, designers, factories and warehouses. And fast fashion faces criticism for encouraging people to buy and throw away more clothes. Speed is a tool, not a virtue.

cards.title: Now it's a bakery chain.
body: You run ten bakeries supplied by one central kitchen. Bread sells steadily. New pastries are hit or miss, and unsold ones are thrown out at night.
How should the kitchen plan pastries?

options.text: Bake all pastries overnight in one big batch to keep costs low
options.feedback: Each pastry costs less to make, but you commit before you know what sells, so waste can wipe out the savings.

options.text: Bake bread overnight; send pastries in two smaller runs based on morning sales
options.feedback: Steady bread stays cheap, and the afternoon run follows real demand. You pay for an extra delivery to waste less.

options.text: Stop new pastries and sell only what you can forecast
options.feedback: Waste drops, but so does the variety that brings customers back. You avoid the guess by giving up the upside.

cards.title: When demand is hard to predict, shorten the wait.
body: Better forecasts help, but a shorter lead time means you need to forecast less. Pay for speed where demand is uncertain, and stay cheap where it is steady.
**Try it today:** list your products. Mark each one steady or unpredictable. For the unpredictable ones, write down how far ahead you commit.
